knowledge_entries.title: Overall Resume Structure
knowledge_entries.content: A strong resume follows a predictable order that both Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and human recruiters can parse quickly: (1) Name and contact information, (2) Professional summary, (3) Skills, (4) Work experience (reverse-chronological), (5) Education, (6) Certifications and projects. Keep entry-level resumes to one page; experienced professionals may use two pages maximum.
knowledge_entries.keywords: resume overall resume structure structure writing guidelines tips
knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Professional Summary
knowledge_entries.content: Open with a 2-4 sentence professional summary (not an 'Objective' statement) that highlights your role identity, years of experience, top 2-3 relevant skills, and a notable achievement. Mirror keywords from the target job description naturally. Example: 'Results-driven backend developer with 3 years of experience building RESTful APIs with Python and FastAPI, reducing endpoint latency by 40%.'
knowledge_entries.keywords: resume professional summary structure writing guidelines tips
knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Work Experience Bullets
knowledge_entries.content: Write each experience entry as 3-6 bullet points starting with strong action verbs (developed, designed, led, optimized, automated, resolved) and quantify results whenever possible using numbers, percentages, or timeframes. Bad: 'Responsible for testing.' Good: 'Built an automated test suite with Selenium covering 85% of core workflows, cutting regression testing time from 2 days to 3 hours.'
knowledge_entries.keywords: resume work experience bullets content writing guidelines tips
knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Action Verbs Library
knowledge_entries.content: Use varied, powerful action verbs to open bullet points: achieved, built, created, delivered, deployed, designed, developed, engineered, executed, implemented, improved, launched, led, managed, negotiated, optimized, performed, reduced, researched, resolved, spearheaded, streamlined, transformed, validated. Avoid weak openers like 'responsible for', 'helped with', or 'worked on'.

knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Tailoring to the Job Description
knowledge_entries.content: ATS software scans resumes for keywords taken directly from the job posting and ranks candidates by match. Study the job description and weave its specific skills and phrases into your summary, skills section, and experience bullets. Include both the acronym and full form (e.g., 'CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery)'). Only include keywords for skills you genuinely possess; never misrepresent experience, as recruiters verify qualifications in interviews.

knowledge_entries.title: ATS-Friendly Formatting
knowledge_entries.content: Around 99% of Fortune 500 companies use ATS software, and roughly 75% of qualified candidates are rejected purely for formatting problems. Follow these rules: use a simple single-column layout; use standard section headings ('Work Experience', 'Skills', 'Education'); avoid headers/footers, tables, text boxes, columns, images, icons, and graphics; choose ATS-friendly fonts (Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman, 10-12pt); and submit as .docx or PDF per application instructions. Complex formatting can shift, hide, or prevent parsing of resume content entirely.
knowledge_entries.keywords: resume ats-friendly formatting formatting writing guidelines tips
knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Skills Section Strategy
knowledge_entries.content: Maintain a dedicated 'Skills' section listing 8-15 hard skills relevant to the target role, grouped logically (e.g., 'Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL; Tools: Git, Docker, AWS'). Add soft skills sparingly and only when the job description asks for them. Do not use skill ratings or progress bars; they are meaningless to ATS systems and recruiters.

knowledge_entries.source: Seed: resume_guidelines_data.py (Indeed ATS guide, university career centers)

knowledge_entries.title: Education & Certifications
knowledge_entries.content: List degrees with institution name, location, degree title, and graduation date (or expected date). Recent graduates can add GPA (if 3.5+) and relevant coursework. Place certifications (AWS, PMP, Security+, etc.) in a dedicated section with the issuing body and date; they are heavily weighted keywords in ATS rankings.

knowledge_entries.title: Projects Section
knowledge_entries.content: For students and career-changers, a Projects section can substitute for work experience. List 2-4 projects with a one-line description, technologies used, and a GitHub or live-demo link. Treat projects like jobs: what did you build, with what tools, and what measurable outcome did it achieve?

knowledge_entries.title: Proofreading & Quality Control
knowledge_entries.content: A single typo can signal carelessness to a recruiter. Proofread with a spell checker and a second reader, read the resume aloud, and verify: consistent dates and verb tenses, correct company names, working links, a professional email address (no nicknames), and an up-to-date LinkedIn or portfolio link. Save a new tailored version for every application instead of reusing one generic file.

knowledge_entries.title: What to Exclude
knowledge_entries.content: Remove from your resume: photos (in most countries), age, marital status, religion, full street address (city is enough), references or 'references available upon request', outdated skills (e.g., MS-DOS), irrelevant hobbies, and unexplained employment gaps (address gaps briefly and honestly if asked). Keep contact information minimal: phone, email, city, LinkedIn, portfolio.

knowledge_entries.title: Common Resume Mistakes
knowledge_entries.content: The most frequent resume mistakes: (1) generic one-size-fits-all resumes; (2) focusing on duties instead of achievements; (3) spelling and grammar errors; (4) cluttered, multi-column layouts; (5) missing keywords from the job posting; (6) exaggerating or fabricating experience; (7) overly long resumes; (8) outdated objective statements; (9) burying the most impressive achievement; and (10) submitting as an image or unsupported file type.

knowledge_entries.title: Student & Entry-Level Resumes
knowledge_entries.content: Students should lead with Education, then Projects, then Experience (internships, part-time jobs), then Skills and Certifications. Extracurricular leadership, hackathon participation, open-source contributions, and relevant coursework are all legitimate resume content. Quantify anything you can ('mentored 10 junior members', 'raised $2,000'). Part-time non-technical jobs still demonstrate soft skills like teamwork and time management.

knowledge_entries.title: Career-Changer Resumes
knowledge_entries.content: Career changers should use a functional or hybrid format that leads with a strong summary and transferable skills. Emphasize completed courses, certifications, portfolio projects, and freelance work in the new field. Map old experience to new requirements explicitly (e.g., 'customer service -> requirements gathering and stakeholder communication'). A well-documented GitHub portfolio is the best proof of new competence.
